summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. No such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap for a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read in public and at the border under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment has been in place since 2007. The Ministry for Justice and Equality is the department that has spoken publicly about bias-motivated abuse.

Hate-crime law is a live protection. An amendment to the Crimes Act 2011, passed on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October 2013, made hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation criminal offences. In July 2026 Parliament passed a further bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to bring transgender identity within those protections. Whether the 2026 provisions have been charged or prosecuted is not sourced here.

Conversion therapy is prohibited: in July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise it. A visitor considering local care should treat any offer of such practice as unlawful.

Relationship recognition is settled. Civil partnerships have existed since 2014 and same-sex marriage has been available since December 2016, when the enabling bill passed unanimously. A spouse or partner travelling with a trans visitor is recognised as such under local law.

Social climate carries documented friction. Following an incident of anti-gay abuse in July 2021, the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would consider legislation to tackle what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' circulating on social media during Pride month; the sourced material also notes a proposal then under investigation to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence.
tangentialFactors:
The 2016 marriage reform did not arrive without contention. A December 2015 consultation on amending the Civil Marriage Act left Gibraltarians polarised, and press coverage of 15 August 2016 records a government minister presiding over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints before the draft bill went to Parliament, with popular consultation and the main parties indicating support for the change.

External accountability expectations form part of the background. The United Kingdom House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's Seventh Report of 2007-08 on Overseas Territories sets standards of good governance and accountability that apply to Gibraltar as an overseas territory, and the Committee's 2008 enquiry recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal across overseas territories.

The pace of protection differs by ground. Sexual orientation hatred and harassment became criminal offences in October 2013, while transgender identity entered the hate crime and hate speech framework only with the July 2026 bill, leaving thirteen years in which conduct motivated by anti-trans hatred fell outside those specific provisions.
localsOnly:
Family law has moved substantially for residents. On 10 April 2013 the Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for want of legal recognition of their relationship challenged the law; Parliament then amended the position through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology.

Sexual activity between men was decriminalised in 1993, and the age of consent was equalised at 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional; the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16 that took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that reform gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. Equal adoption rights for same-sex couples date from a Supreme Court ruling of 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the July 2026 hate crime and hate speech provisions covering transgender identity have been charged or prosecuted is unresolved in the sourced material; only their passage by Parliament is recorded.

Whether the proposal reported in July 2021 to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence was ever enacted is unresolved here.

Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 has been extended to Gibraltar by Order in Council is unresolved; no extension appears in the sourced material, and the territory's own rules on single-sex services and facilities are not covered by any source.

Gibraltar's gender-recognition position is stated in the sourced material as a prohibition on changing legal gender, but the underlying statutory or constitutional provision is not identified, so the precise legal basis remains unresolved.

Several factual claims, including the 2013, 2016 and 2026 legislative dates, rest on encyclopaedic accounts and a Wikipedia-derived mirror rather than on primary legal texts; independent verification of those dates against the legislation itself is not carried out here.

The Foreign Affairs Committee report also records corruption concerns in Turks and Caicos; that material concerns a different overseas territory and carries no bearing on Gibraltar.
